The Authentic Name

Why ištar.com is the correct form

Mesopotamian Original

Ištar

The name in its original Mesopotamian form. The original script is preserved in scholarly transliteration systems.

ASCII Constraint

ISHTAR

Stripped of its identity, the name was reduced to plain Latin letters. The original orthography — stress, length, breathing — was erased by systems that only understand A-Z.

Unicode Restoration

Ištar

The Unicode restoration recovers what ASCII destroyed. This is philological accuracy — not decoration. The domain encodes to Punycode, but the browser displays the truth.

Valid Scholarly Variations
ištar Ishtar Inanna

Each variant is an attested scholarly orthography. The owned form is the active domain; others are historically valid alternatives.

Punycode Encoding
ištar.com → xn--itar-g6a.com

The non-ASCII characters in Ištar are encoded while the ASCII remains visible. To the DNS, it is Punycode. To humanity, it is Ištar.

Etymology

The deep ancestry of Ištar

Unknown unknown "Lady of Heaven"

The divine name Ištar is not Semitic in origin and likely derives from a Sumerian divine title associated with the planet Venus; it became the Akkadian goddess of love, war, and the morning/evening star

06

Mythology & Lore

Lady of Heaven, queen of love and war

Ištar (Akkadian) and Inanna (Sumerian) are the most prominent goddesses of Mesopotamia, ruling love, sexuality, fertility, war, and the planet Venus. Hymns praise her as both the life-giving morning star and the terrible warrior who rides into battle.

The most famous myth is Ištar's Descent to the Underworld. She descends to the realm of her sister Ereškigal, is stripped of her divine powers at seven gates, and is killed. Her servant Ninšubur secures her rescue, but the underworld demands a substitute: her husband Tammuz (Dumuzid), the shepherd god of vegetation, who spends half the year in the underworld.

In the Epic of Gilgameš, Ištar proposes marriage to the hero Gilgameš. When he refuses and catalogues her destructive former lovers, she demands the Bull of Heaven from her father Anu and sends it to ravage Uruk. Gilgameš and Enkidu slay the bull, setting in motion Enkidu's fatal punishment.

07

Pronunciation

How to say the name

Akkadian: /ˈiʃtar/, with the initial consonant pronounced like English sh. The š (S-caron) is the standard scholarly way to write this sound when the original cuneiform does not use the Latin alphabet.

Modern English usually says ISH-tar. The Unicode restoration Ištar keeps the single character that signals the original /ʃ/ sound — a precision that Ishtar can only approximate with two letters.

09

Syncretism

Ištar across cultures

Sumerian Inanna: Ištar is the direct Akkadian continuation of Inanna, the earlier Sumerian goddess of love and war. The two share myths, titles, and iconography so closely that scholars often treat them as a single complex.

Phoenician Astarte and Syrian Atargatis: West Semitic ʿAštart (Astarte) and later Atargatis are close cognates, spreading Ištar's cult across the Levant and Mediterranean. The Greek Aphrodītē and Roman Venus absorbed aspects of her as goddess of love, while the Greek Ártemis and Roman Diana absorbed her warrior side.

Egyptian Isis: During the Greco-Roman period, Ištar/Astarte was frequently syncretized with Isis, another powerful goddess of love, magic, and cosmic queenship. Both were invoked across the ancient world as mistresses of heaven and sea.

10

Cultural Legacy

From Babylon to book and screen

Ištar's most famous monument is the Ishtar Gate of Babylon, a blue-glazed Processional Way guarded by lions, bulls, and dragons. Fragments now reside in museums from Berlin to New York, making her one of the most visually recognizable deities of the ancient Near East.

Her name echoes in the Biblical Esther and possibly in the festival of Easter (a contested but persistent folk etymology). Today she appears in fantasy literature, games, and neopagan devotion as the original warrior-queen of heaven.
